This essay brings those stories together and asks what they make possible next. As AI changes how films are made, the human relationships, shared work and community benefits of a production become more important. How can we design that giving into filmmaking from the start? Full Essay Below “We wanted to make clear that we’re not coming here just to make a movie and go away. We were creating something that was going to live beyond the film.” Vinati Makijany, Producer, Skater Girl Women’s Media Center, June 2021 In this essay A word about the films themselves The hundred years between The modern renaissance The thing no one named Why now The next hundred years New Jersey, and the open hand Author’s note In 1921, on the film lots scattered across a Los Angeles that was still mostly orange groves and open light, the most famous woman in the world carried a bucket from set to set. It was a small galvanized pail with a little flag on it, and Mary Pickford brought it to the people who were working that day and asked them to put in whatever they could. She did not need the money. She was the most bankable star alive, a founder of her own studio, a woman who had negotiated against the men who ran Hollywood and won. But she had watched what happened to the others when a picture wrapped and the checks stopped: the carpenters, the extras, the electricians, the people whose names the audience would never learn, who built the thing the audience came to see and then went home to nothing. So she passed the bucket. The coins inside it became a fund, and the fund became a house with a hospital, set among walnut and orange groves in Woodland Hills, where film people who had nowhere else to go could grow old among their own. It is still there, and it still takes them in. Pickford insisted it be called a House and not a Home, because actors, she said, are only ever between engagements. A hundred years later, on the other side of the earth, a small crew arrived in a village in the desert of Rajasthan to make a film about a girl who wanted to skate. Before they shot a single frame, financing the film independently out of their own pockets, they built the village a skatepark. Concrete and permanent and free, fourteen and a half thousand square feet of it, one of the largest in India and the first that part of Rajasthan had ever seen. Concrete and permanent and free, fourteen and a half thousand square feet of it, one of the largest in India and the first that part of Rajasthan had ever seen. They had gone looking with a second agenda that film productions almost never carry: not only a place to shoot, but land to build on. Fifteen days of driving, and the village that settled it was the one where the children had already made their own skateboards. The film is called Skater Girl . It did what films do, it was watched, and loved by many, and folded into the endless stream of things to watch. But the thing it left behind did not stream and did not fade. The trucks pulled away in 2019. The skatepark is still there, and the children of Khempur are still on it. Four of them, most leaving the village for the first time in their lives, went on to skate for Rajasthan at a national championship. Mary Pickford and the people who made Skater Girl never knew of one another. A century stands between them, and an ocean, and almost everything else. They shared no movement, no manifesto, no word for what they were doing. One passed a bucket so that film workers would have somewhere to grow old. The other poured a slab so that children in a village would have somewhere to fly. And yet something connects them across all that distance: a love of film and a love of people, and an instinct that filmmaking might be turned toward both at once. Hundreds of others felt the same instinct, across the long century between the bucket and the slab. A star endowing a relief fund. A director turning a film’s profits into a foundation. A crew keeping a struck set out of the landfill. A production that employed a town so completely the town was never quite the same. A company built, against every incentive of the industry, on the belief that a story well told could move the world to act. Many of them knew one another, learned from one another, gave to the same funds. What no one had done was name the thing they shared, and a name is no small thing: it is what turns a hundred years of generous acts into a tradition, something a field can see itself in, learn from, and carry forward on purpose. This is the Filmanthropy Ledger: a century of giving through film, gathered as one connected tradition. It is a record of what people have done and an argument about what we could do next. As AI changes how films are made, this hundred-year instinct takes on new significance. AI can generate moving images without a conventional shoot: no town hosting a crew, no set built and struck, no shared afternoon on location. And the moment that becomes possible is the exact moment the other thing, the real places touched and the real lives changed in the course of making something together, stops being a nice side effect and becomes the whole point, the one part no machine can counterfeit. If the making of a film can be designed, on purpose, from the very first day, to leave its people and its places better than it found them, then what could the next hundred years of filmmaking actually build, and what would it take to decide, now, to build it that way? A word about the films themselves The films are already gifts. This needs saying once, clearly, so nothing that follows is mistaken for an argument against the art. Casablanca gave the world something real simply by being made well and loved widely. So did Singin’ in the Rain, and Star Wars, and ten thousand others whose fundamental gift was to be wonderful, and for whom that was more than enough. A film that moves millions of strangers to laugh in the same dark room, or to forgive someone, or to imagine a life they had not imagined, has given a gift that needs no further justification. That is the oldest generosity of cinema, and the largest, and this record takes it entirely as given. Our subject lies alongside it: the giving that happens in and around the making, the part that touches the people and places a production reaches and never appears on the screen at all. The art is one kind of gift. This is the record of the other kinds. The hundred years between It began not with a grand gesture but with a practical one. Mutual aid Pickford’s relief fund, incorporated in 1921, was mutual aid, not charity in the soft sense: built by the people of an industry for the people of that industry, in an era with no other safety net. It began, by the Fund’s own account, with a simple coin box on the studio floors. By 1932, in the worst of the Depression, it had become a payroll pledge: a half of one percent of the studio paychecks of those who could spare it, set aside for those who could not. A private social security for film workers, invented by film workers, a decade before the public one existed. Three years after Pickford’s first bucket, the same instinct surfaced an ocean away, with no coordination at all. British film people founded the Cinematograph Trade Benevolent Fund in London in 1924, for exactly the same reason, to care for the workers of their own young industry when hard luck took the work away. It still exists, a century on, under a newer name, and it still runs a care home. Since 1946 a single glittering night, the Royal Film Performance, has paid for it, turning the premiere of a major film into an act of giving to the people behind the scenes. Nobody in London was copying Los Angeles. The need was universal, and so was the response. Then came the war. In October 1942, the actor John Garfield sat down beside Bette Davis in the Warner Bros. commissary and said something ought to be done for the servicemen pouring through Los Angeles on their way to the Pacific. Davis agreed, and the two of them built it: the Hollywood Canteen, in a converted stable on Cahuenga Boulevard, where any serviceman or woman in uniform got in free, ate for free, and might be served a sandwich by a movie star and pulled onto the dance floor by another. No officers, Garfield insisted, and no segregation by rank or race. Nearly four million came through the doors in three years. The stars washed dishes and bused tables, and the profits of two films made about the place were poured back into running it. When the Canteen closed on Thanksgiving Day of 1945, the half a million dollars left in the bank was given to the relief of the men and women it had served. It was the gift economy of the film set, opened up and pointed outward. The film becomes the gift Then the instinct learned the trick that would matter most: a film could be made into the gift itself, not merely the thing that paid for one. In 1954, at the height of his fame, the comedian Danny Kaye became the first Goodwill Ambassador for the young United Nations children’s fund, a role he held for thirty-three years, until he died. He made a film, Assignment: Children, underwritten by Paramount, every dollar of profit given to the fund, and it reached more than a hundred million people. Kaye put the spirit of it better than any definition could. Politics don’t count where children are concerned, he said. How can you love an Israeli child and not an Arab child, a North Korean child and not a South Korean child. It’s impossible. What Kaye began, others took up, and the taking-up is the thread itself, because each was handed the impulse by the one before. Audrey Hepburn had been a half-starved child in occupied Holland, kept alive in part by international relief; she became the fund’s ambassador in 1988 and gave the last five years of her life to it, saying plainly that the aid she once received was why she went. And when Roger Moore, who had played James Bond, was asked what moved him to the same work, he did not reach for a grand reason. His curiosity got the better of him, he said, after his friend Audrey Hepburn introduced him to it. He went to a meeting with her and stayed for the rest of his life. His curiosity got the better of him, he said, after his friend Audrey Hepburn introduced him to it. He went to a meeting with her and stayed for the rest of his life. Kaye to Hepburn to Moore: three actors, three decades, one thread, each pulled in by the hand of the one before. The impulse was never an abstraction. It traveled person to person, the way most true things do. Fame as an instrument It traveled into other rooms and changed shape as it went. In 1982 Paul Newman began bottling his own salad dressing as a joke and a dare, gave every cent of the profit away, and kept giving until it passed six hundred million dollars. A movie star’s hobby had become one of the quietly radical ideas in American business: a company that exists only to give itself away. He was embarrassed, he said, that the dressing was outgrossing his films. The model was good enough that more than two dozen other companies copied it outright, and a generation of his peers pointed to him as the reason they gave at all. Elizabeth Taylor took the idea somewhere harder. In 1985, watching a plague move through her own community while the country looked away, she decided her fame was the only tool equal to the silence and became the first major star to stand up for people dying of AIDS, raising money and breaking the shame around the disease at a moment when almost no one of her stature would say its name aloud. I resented my fame, she said, until I realized I could use it. Never only American In India, the actor Aamir Khan turned a television program about his country’s miseries into the Paani Foundation and sent thousands of villages into a competition to build their own watersheds, helping turn drought-cracked land green again across Maharashtra. In China, the martial-arts star Jet Li nearly drowned with his small daughters in the 2004 tsunami and came out of the water changed, building what became one of the first private charitable foundations his country had ever allowed, on the arithmetic that one person and one dollar and one month could add up to one enormous family. Jackie Chan, who had wanted only to be famous and rich, said his friends taught him to give and now he could not stop; he built schools across the remote interior of China. In Britain, a screenwriter came home from the 1985 Ethiopian famine and founded Comic Relief, and over forty years the comedians and filmmakers of one country made the public laugh into giving more than a billion and a half pounds. The thread ran through every film culture on earth, under a hundred flags, almost never under a shared name. When it did not work It did not always work, and the honest record says so. Brad Pitt set out after Hurricane Katrina to rebuild the homes of the Lower Ninth Ward in New Orleans. He meant it with his whole heart, and he hired great architects, and the houses began to rot and leak and fail, and the families he meant to help ended up in court, and a promised settlement collapsed when the money behind it proved not to be there. We went into it incredibly naive, he said, years later. He had asked the right question and gotten the answer terribly wrong. When the Brazilian film City of God cast the real young people of a real Rio favela and made them stars for a season, it changed some of their lives and left others almost exactly where it found them. One of them said plainly that the film had brought the favela no good at all. These are not failures of instinct. They are failures of execution, and they belong here as surely as the triumphs, because a field that cannot look honestly at its near misses and its collapses is not a field. It is a brochure. The problem is never the wanting. It is the design. None of this was a gap. A relief fund in 1921, a benevolent fund in 1924, a wartime canteen in 1942, a film made to give in 1954 and the long human chain that followed it, a company built to give itself away in 1982, a star who broke a silence in 1985: a whole world of givers, real and continuous, reaching across the century. The thread was there the whole time. What it never had was a name to make it legible as one thing, so each generation built from instinct rather than from the one before, and began again where someone else had already arrived. The modern renaissance By the end of the twentieth century the scattered instinct began to organize into something more deliberate, a renaissance of about thirty years in which people began not only to do this work but to build it into the machinery of production, to study it as a subject, and at last to give a piece of it a name. Three things were happening at once, and Social Effects exists to celebrate all three and to build on them. The operators The first was a new kind of operator, who looked at the sheer physical wreckage of a production, the tons of material and food and the built worlds struck and dumped the moment the camera stopped, and asked whether the making itself could be turned toward good. They worked out the answers with their own hands, and they are the forerunners of this whole field. In 1991, Syd Mandelbaum, the son of Holocaust survivors, stood backstage at a concert and watched untouched food thrown away by the ton while people went hungry a few miles down the road. He had come home from the first World Gathering of Jewish Holocaust Survivors with something burning in him that would not go out, a sense that he had to do something to change the world. His answer was Rock and Wrap It Up .

He had come home from the first World Gathering of Jewish Holocaust Survivors with something burning in him that would not go out, a sense that he had to do something to change the world. His answer was Rock and Wrap It Up . It began with concert food and grew into a discipline: the contractual rider that says prepared food which was never served does not go to the landfill, it goes to people. He took it to film and television sets, to sports arenas, to hotels and schools. Over the decades his model has recovered, by the organization's own count, the equivalent of more than a billion meals, and the language he drafted became the basis of a 2008 federal law encouraging the government to donate its own surplus food rather than throw it away. Eva Radke took up the next part of the problem in a Brooklyn warehouse in 2008. She had worked in the art departments of productions and could not stop seeing what got thrown away when a set came down, the lumber and the furniture and the paint, whole rooms of usable material dumped because no one had made the place that would catch it. So she made it. Film Biz Recycling, eleven thousand square feet, where productions could send their struck sets instead of the dump, and most of what came in went back out to charities, schools, and theater companies. She diverted six hundred tons over seven years and won an Environmental Protection Agency award for it. Then, in 2015, the Brooklyn warehouse closed, because the retail floor could not cover the last hundred thousand a year and the foundation world did not yet know how to fund a thing that looked like a thrift store and acted like a public utility. She called that closing watching a unicorn die. But the work did not die with the warehouse. The name reopened in Savannah and still does its job, and the deeper engine she had been building alongside it, ArtCube Nation, a worldwide network of the makers and art-department crews who catch what productions discard, is still going strong two decades on. Obi-Wan and Dumbledore, she said, were stronger in death, and maybe her impact would be felt more once the thing itself was gone. She was right, and then some: the people who came after learned from what she made and from what it cost her, while she simply kept building. docs.text: In 2009, out of a film shoot in Minnesota where she and a colleague diverted eleven tons of waste in ten weeks, Shannon Schaefer Bart founded EcoSet and created the on-set role that had never quite existed, the person whose whole job is to make sure the production gives back what it cannot use. With Kris Barberg, who now runs it, EcoSet turned set surplus into a standing operation: a Los Angeles warehouse where nonprofits and families take what they need for free, diversion rates that reach into the high nineties, and millions of dollars of reusable goods moved out of the waste stream and back into the community. Bart’s work was so thoroughly the future that the future hired her; she is now at Netflix, helping make production sustainability the default across one of the largest content engines on earth. On the East Coast, beginning in 2013, Emellie O’Brien and Earth Angel made the same case in the same years, turning the greening of a film set from a footnote into a profession. Their full records open this Ledger’s entries below. The scholars The second thing was that serious people began to study film-for-good as a field rather than a scatter of one-off projects. The most careful of that work came out of UCLA, at the Skoll Center, endowed in 2014 by a ten-million-dollar gift from Jeff Skoll, who had founded Participant Media on the conviction that a well-told story could be a force in the world. In 2019 the Center published The State of Social Impact Entertainment, a rigorous attempt to map the narrative film, documentary, television, and theater that engage audiences in the world’s problems, and to give that work a history and a set of best practices. It called itself the field’s first such report and promised others; none has yet followed, which leaves it standing, years on, as the one serious map of its kind. It charts that ground with care, the ground of what a finished film says to the people who watch it. This Ledger travels a second axis. The word The third thing was that a piece of the field finally got a name. The word is Filmanthropy, film and philanthropy joined on purpose. As far as the public record shows, it was introduced around 2007 and 2008 by Ted Leonsis, the media entrepreneur behind the documentary platform SnagFilms, who used it for films aimed at the causes the world most needs to face. He built the word, and the credit is his. Others picked it up and carried it, each in a different place and for a different reason: a festival in Los Angeles that took the name in 2009 to honor filmmakers working for a better world, a producer in Dallas who used it for films made to raise money for a cause, a social enterprise in London that took it in 2017 for its work teaching participatory filmmaking, a foundation in Burbank that took it in 2020 to support people in the industry. Each was a real effort by real people, and each gave the word meaning long before the field these pages describe had been seen who

Each was a real effort by real people, and each gave the word meaning long before the field these pages describe had been seen whole. These are the shoulders this Ledger stands on: the operators who built the infrastructure, the scholars who studied the work, the namers who gave a piece of it a word. The renaissance was real. It happened across decades and across very different kinds of work, and it was not yet understood as one coherent and various tradition. The thing no one named Stand back far enough and the pattern is undeniable. A relief fund in 1921 and a skatepark in 2018 are the same gesture, made a century and an ocean apart. And yet no account had ever drawn the full line between them, because the people best placed to draw it were each looking at a different part. The scholars charted what a finished film says to its audience: the documentary that changes a law, the drama that shifts a public mood. The word, in nearly every hand that held it, meant the same thing, film as advocacy, the finished film pointed at a cause. That is a true and valuable axis, and it names one real strand of everything in these pages. But it does not reach the bucket on Pickford’s set, or the half a million dollars left in the Canteen’s bank, or the six hundred tons Eva Radke kept out of the landfill, or the skatepark left standing in the desert. None of those is a message. They are gifts the making left behind, in the people and the places a production touches, whether or not the finished film ever says a word. That is the second axis, and it had no map. That is not a small oversight. A practice that cannot see itself cannot teach itself to the next generation, cannot become a discipline with standards and a memory. The thread existed. What it still needed was to be seen whole, and named, so it could become a tradition someone could build on. What this record sets out to do is modest and specific, and worth stating without inflation. Not to invent a word, because the word already exists and is good, and inventing a replacement would only hide the debt owed to everyone who carried it first. The work is to take the existing word and widen it to fit the whole field at last, to say that Filmanthropy is not only film as advocacy but every way the love of film and the love of humanity meet, whether proceeds, materials, presence, equity, the change a story works in the people who watch it, or something permanent left behind. And then to name the cutting edge the word had never reached, the part the rest of these pages are really about: not the giving a production remembers on its way out, but the giving it is built around from the start. Why now This Ledger arrives now, and not ten years ago or ten years from now, for two reasons. The first is that the founding era of the field is ending in plain sight, just as it becomes visible. The second is harder to see, and it changes everything. An era closing Participant, which carried Filmanthropy in its advocacy sense further than any company before it, and proved along the way that conscience and a balance sheet could coexist, closed in 2024 after twenty years and a wall of Academy Awards. Some of the founding generation of practitioners, the people who built the first recycling warehouses and the first on-set sustainability crews, are still alive and still working, and have never once been interviewed as part of a connected story, because the connected story did not exist to interview them for. The institution that grew from Pickford’s bucket has just passed its hundredth birthday. The founding chapter is closing at the very moment the book about it can finally be written. That window is open now, and it will not stay open. The artifact and the event For the entire century this record describes, one thing was always true and never had to be said: to get the film, you had to make it. You had to go somewhere real, with real people, and do the thing. The finished film was the visible part, the artifact that streamed and was reviewed and won or lost a weekend. But the artifact was never the whole of it. The work was also the months an actor spent becoming someone else, the town that hosted the shoot, the village a crew built on location, the people changed by having been in the room. The film was the artifact. The making was the event. And you could not have the first without the second. That assumption is now coming loose. Artificial intelligence has begun to produce the artifact without the event. A feature-length film generated almost entirely by AI, with no cast and no crew and no cameras, has been accepted into a major festival for the first time. Synthetic performers are being built and marketed as the next generation of movie stars. The question the next century of filmmaking has to answer, then, is no longer how to make the artifact. The machine can produce the artifact. The question is what, in the making of films, cannot be generated, and the honest answer runs in two directions at once. Outward, toward the world the film passes through. A model can produce a convincing image of a place, but it cannot give anything back to one, because it was never in one. It cannot employ a town, or spend an afternoon with a community, or leave a skatepark behind. Everything this record has gathered lives in that direction, and none of it can be simulated, because all of it depends on having actually happened, somewhere, to someone. Inward, toward the people who do the making. A model can produce a performance, but it cannot undergo one. It was never on the set before dawn, never afraid, never changed by the months of work alongside other people. You do not simply make a film, you go through one, and the people who go through it come out altered. That, too, is a kind of giving, the kind a production makes to its own, and it is as far beyond a prompt as the skatepark is, for the same reason. The model has no afternoon to spend and no self to transform. As the artifact becomes abundant and instant, then, the worth of a film does not vanish. It moves toward the event the artifact was only ever the trace of, toward everything that had to actually happen, to real people in a real place, before there was anything to watch at all. The next hundred years The future of this field is not a defense against the machine. It is something more hopeful, a clarification, forced into the open by the very technology that seemed to threaten it. Regenerative There is a word, borrowed from agriculture and design and economics, that names the shape of the hope. Regenerative. It was coined by people who found sustainable too small for what they meant. To sustain is to maintain, to do less harm, to leave a system no worse than you found it. To regenerate is to leave it actively better, more alive than before. One of the farmers who helped coin the term put it plainly: people do not want a world that is merely sustained, they want one that is getting better. Read as a brief for a film shoot, that becomes a definition worth keeping: a regenerative production is one that leaves the people and the place that hosted it better off than if the film had never come. A traditional production arrives, takes what it needs, and leaves, and what it leaves behind is an afterthought at best, a row of full dumpsters at worst. A regenerative production designs the giving in from the first day, before a frame is shot. Surplus is rehomed, skills are shared, the young people of the place are brought onto a real set, and the cast and crew are given a real stake in the thing they made. The material that would have been wasted becomes something the community keeps. At its furthest reach, the production leaves something permanent. The giving is built into the making, with intention, from the start. This is why the arrival of AI, which frightens so many, may be the moment the field comes into its own. When the artifact is free, the event is everything. When anyone can generate the image of a town, the production that actually employed one, fed one, and built something lasting in one becomes not the old way of doing things but the valuable way, the human way, rooted in the physical and social world and impossible to copy out of it. The tools will keep getting better, and they should. The work of making a film with other people, in a real place, for the lasting good of that place and the people in it, will keep being something only people can do. There is an older idea underneath all of this. You do not change the world by fighting the thing you want to replace. You change it by building a new model that makes the old one obsolete. This record is not an argument against the way films have always been made. It is the account of a better way that has been building itself for a hundred years, in scattered pieces, under no single name, and an invitation to see those pieces as one thing at last, and to build the next hundred years of it on purpose. Where American film began American film did not begin in Hollywood. It began in New Jersey, in Thomas Edison’s studios just west of New York and then on the cliffs of Fort Lee, the country’s first film town, where the studios clustered before the industry chased the sun west and forgot the place it came from. A hundred years later the cameras are coming back, drawn by new studios and soundstages and incentives into towns that have not hosted a production in generations. The industry is returning to its birthplace with a chance to decide, this time, at the beginning, what kind of industry to build. That opportunity is not only New Jersey’s. The cases in these pages were built in Los Angeles and London, in Rajasthan and New Zealand, in a Brooklyn warehouse and a Minnesota winter, in Mumbai and Rio and the interior of China. The open hand New Jersey can be the place that goes first. A production arriving in a New Jersey town is a temporary institution of real wealth and real power, landing in a community, employing it, using its spaces, and then leaving. The only question, the one this whole record has circled, is what it leaves, and whether the leaving was designed or left to chance. It can leave the town as it found it. It can leave it a little worse. Or it can be built so that the making itself is a gift, the town left more whole than the production found it, and the people who made the film left changed by having made it that way. That choice is in front of New Jersey now, and in front of every place the cameras go. What it could look like So picture the largest version of it, because the largest version is the one that makes the case. A major film comes to New Jersey. Not a modest independent feature but a tentpole, the kind of production that costs as much as a small city’s annual budget, half a billion dollars, with the spectacle and the stars and the opening weekend that a number like that demands. By any ordinary measure it is one of the largest economic events the region will host that year. The ordinary measure is also the whole problem. A production that size moves through a place like weather: it rents what it needs, hires for the duration, spends enormous sums in a few months, and then the trucks pull away and the place settles back to what it was, a little richer for a season and otherwise unchanged. The money was real. It simply passed through. Now imagine the same half a billion dollars, the same movie, every spectacular frame of it intact, with one decision made before the first day of construction: that the budget would be routed, wherever it could be, so that spending it built something that stayed. This is not a smaller film or a worthier one. It is the same blockbuster, run through a different plumbing. The sets are the clearest case. A production of this scale builds whole worlds and, by long habit, sends them to the landfill at wrap. Designed the other way, the structures go up to last, engineered from the first blueprint to become buildings the place will keep, on land held by a community land trust so the value cannot be quietly bought out from under it a decade later, the way value usually is. As far as the public record shows, the word was introduced around 2007 and 2008 by Ted Leonsis , a media entrepreneur and the founder of the documentary platform SnagFilms, which he built alongside Steve Case, Miles Gilburne, and chief executive Rick Allen. SnagFilms launched in the summer of 2008 with a catalog of documentaries and an invitation to audiences to become a filmanthropist by helping good films find an audience. Leonsis used the word to describe film aimed at the issues the world most needs to face. He built the word himself, and we are glad to say so plainly. The People Who Carried It A word only lives if people choose to carry it, and several did, in different places and for different reasons. In 2009, the FILManthropy Festival began in the Los Angeles area, founded by Jodi Fung through her nonprofit the Sirens Society, honoring filmmakers who use film to make the world better and raising support for the causes those filmmakers championed. Around the same time, in Dallas, the producer Melina McKinnon and her company M3 Films used the word for filmmaking made deliberately to raise awareness and funds for a cause. The term moved through the documentary world. Pat Mitchell , the first woman to lead PBS and later the head of the Paley Center for Media, used it. Jeff Skoll , the founder of Participant Media, the most influential company ever built around films with a social purpose, engaged with it in the philanthropy press. Filmmakers and critics debated it on festival panels, and journalists carried it into print. In 2017, Fisayo Fadahunsi founded Filmanthropy CIC in London, a community-media social enterprise that uses participatory filmmaking and workshops to build engaged citizens of all ages. In 2020, the Filmanthropy Foundation was established in Burbank, California, a nonprofit supporting creatives and veterans in the film industry. Each of these is a separate effort, built by different people, in different places, with its own mission. Each gave this word meaning and momentum long before Social Effects existed. Inventing a replacement would have hidden our connection to everyone who came before us. By keeping the word, and being clear about the practice we are building within it, we let the lineage stay visible: the same word, a wide field, and our particular place within it. The decks above set out a New Jersey use case. This essay explores the larger possibility behind it: what if the making of a film helped create places, services and opportunities that kept serving people long after production ended? Drawing on the history documented in the Filmanthropy Ledger, it brings those possibilities together at a deliberately ambitious scale. The billion-dollar production imagined below is a thought experiment, distinct from the proposals in the decks. What NJ Can Do Now New Jersey is about to have more film production than at any point in its history. Netflix Fort Monmouth opens in 2028. Paramount 1888 Studios is under construction in Bayonne. Lionsgate is building in Newark. Fifty-eight Film Ready communities are waiting. What if one of those productions, stacking its budget with grants, philanthropy, government funds, and deliberate design, built something for NJ that would still be standing in 50 years? Production Budget + NEA / State Arts Grants + County Economic Dev Funds + Private Philanthropy + Corporate Partners = Something That Stays That’s not a fantasy. That’s a financing structure. And it starts with recognizing the possibilities, daring to dream, and acting on the logic. The pieces already exist Nothing in what follows has to be invented. Every component has already been done, once, by someone, and documented. The only thing that has never been done is to do them all together, in one production, by design. A filmmaker has given the money back. When Steven Spielberg made Schindler’s List he forwent his salary and called the profits blood money, and his share went out into the world through the foundations he then built rather than into his own accounts. docs.text: When Steven Spielberg made Schindler’s List he forwent his salary and called the profits blood money, and his share went out into the world through the foundations he then built rather than into his own accounts. The maker treating the film’s proceeds as something owed to the world is not a hypothetical. It happened on one of the most honored films ever made. A production has built the permanent thing first. The crew of Skater Girl poured a concrete skatepark for a village in Rajasthan before they shot a frame, the largest in India, and it still stands and is still used years after the trucks left. The set has outlived the film. Hobbiton, built for The Lord of the Rings on a New Zealand sheep farm, was rebuilt to last and became a permanent place that now supports the region on its own. The made world that survives the production, and pays its own way afterward, is not a hypothetical either. And a production has come within a single decision of something far greater, and missed. Interstellar planted five hundred acres of real corn for the look of the thing, harvested it, sold it, and the production turned a profit on the crop, and then fed no one with it, because feeding someone was never the plan. The Robin Williams film about Patch Adams brought the world’s attention and real money to a vision of a free hospital, and the hospital was never built, because the film told the story instead of building the thing the story was about. These are the near misses, and they are the most instructive cases of all, because they show how little stood between what happened and what could have happened. A different decision, made earlier, and the corn feeds a county and the hospital gets built. Each of these is a single instrument. What no one has done is play them as one chord. The scale of the problem, and the scale of the answer Set the film down for a moment and look at what New Jersey already spends. The state pours enormous public sums into its mental health crisis every year, and a great deal of it goes to the most expensive and least healing part of the system: emergency rooms holding people who should not be there, repeat hospitalizations, the revolving door between crisis and street and jail that processes human beings at great cost and leaves them no better than it found them. This is money already being spent, every year, with the meter running and nothing owned at the end of it. It is the most expensive way a society can fail to solve a problem. Now bring the film back, at full scale. Not a modest feature but a tentpole, the kind of production that costs as much as a small city’s annual budget. The film is the engine. The infrastructure is the point. And the state’s half is not charity, it is the cheaper option, because owning the solution once costs less over time than renting the failure forever. What could that build, owned outright, never to be lost? What the money buys Begin with the crisis centers. For about four million dollars a New Jersey hospital builds an EmPATH unit, a calm, living-room-style space where a person in crisis is met by clinicians and given dignity and time instead of waiting strapped to the noise of an emergency room. The first ones in the state are opening now. At roughly that figure, and less at smaller hospitals where the unit can be smaller, the production could fund twenty-five of them across New Jersey, a standing statewide network of humane crisis care where today there are almost none. Then the homes. A network of ordinary houses, four and five bedrooms, scattered through the towns of the state and turned into respite homes, places a person can come to stay and steady in a crisis rather than be committed, staffed by peers who have been through it themselves. Say a hundred of them. Bought outright, with the production’s capital, and placed into a community land trust so that they are owned free and clear, forever, by the public purpose they serve. Not leased. Not mortgaged. Owned. A house the trust owns cannot be foreclosed, cannot be sold out from under the people it shelters, cannot be lost to a budget cut or a change of administration. The single most radical thing the money does is also the simplest: it buys the buildings, so no one can ever take them away. Then the teams. New Jersey’s statewide network of mobile crisis responders, the peers and counselors who come to a person in distress rather than waiting for the police to, runs the state roughly sixteen million dollars a year. The part that compounds Here the argument stops being about buildings and starts being about people, because this is where a thing that looks like a cost reveals itself as an engine. Building and running all of this is work, and work is jobs: the trades that build and retrofit the homes and the units, the clinicians and peers who staff them, the crews who maintain them. A capital project of this size is also one of the largest workforce programs a state could run. But the deeper turn is who does that work. The people who come through the system, who stay in the homes and steady in the centers, are the natural staff of the next homes and the next centers. The peer who was helped becomes the peer who helps. The person the old system would have cycled through an emergency room three times a year instead has a place to live, a reason to get up, a community that knows their name, and eventually a job inside the thing that caught them. That is the answer to the two quiet epidemics underneath the loud one. Loneliness, because the homes and the network are a community, not a queue. And recidivism, the revolving door itself, because a person with housing they cannot lose, work that means something, and people around them does not cycle back into crisis and jail at anything like the old rate. The system stops processing people and starts enlisting them. And people who have been caught, in the experience of nearly everyone who builds these things, start giving back on their own, because that is what people do when something real was done for them. The infrastructure does not just hold; it grows its own next generation of builders. Why the money does not run out The objection to anything this large is always the same, and it is fair: a billion dollars builds it, and then what, when the billion is gone? The answer is that the billion is a capital event, not an operating budget, and the operating money already exists. It is being spent right now, by payers who will keep spending it, on exactly this category of need, only today they spend it on the expensive end. Health insurers already reimburse crisis stabilization and behavioral health care; a staffed crisis center and a peer respite home deliver that same reimbursable care at a fraction of what an emergency room and a hospital bed cost, which means the ongoing care is paid for by the payments that were always going to be made. Housing subsidy already flows; vouchers that today pay rent into a private landlord’s pocket can instead service the upkeep of a home the trust already owns, where the only recurring cost is maintenance, which is far cheaper than a mortgage on a building you do not own or rent on one you never will. The film itself earns for decades, the ticket sales and the streaming and the long tail of a movie millions have seen, flowing back to the purpose. And once it visibly works, the ordinary annual giving and public investment that gathers around any proven model arrives on top of all of it, the way money always finds a thing that is already working. So the capital builds and buys the assets, once. The assets are then sustained by money that was already being spent anyway, redirected from renting failure to maintaining what is owned. This is the whole secret, and it is less a feat of finance than a shift of imagination. The instinct is to assume something this large must be impossibly complicated. It is not. Every piece of it already exists and is already funded. EmPATH units are being built. Mobile teams are contracted and running. Insurers reimburse this care. Vouchers pay this rent. Films earn for decades. No one has simply assembled the pieces with a single upfront act that buys the assets outright, so that the recurring streams stop renting and start sustaining. The innovation is the assembly and the ownership. Almost nothing else has to be newly invented. Why it is worth doing even if it fails Let the hardest version of the objection stand: suppose it does not all work. Suppose the film underperforms, or the politics shift, or a third of the plan goes wrong the way Pitt’s houses went wrong and Radke’s warehouse ran out of money. First attempts at hard things miss, and the honest record, which named those failures plainly, will not pretend this one is exempt. Even then, consider what a billion dollars spent this way leaves behind on its worst day. The crisis centers are built and staffed and standing. docs.text: Why filmmaking’s future is human and civic | The Filmanthropy Ledger Skip to the content The Filmanthropy Ledger by Social Effects NJ Read in the Ledger Social Effects NJ Filmanthropy and AI Why filmmaking’s future is human and civic The artifact. The making. The people and places. The Filmanthropy Ledger · Social Effects NJ Artificial intelligence is changing what a film costs, how fast it is made, and what a screen can show. It is worth being clear, then, about the part of filmmaking that does not change, and why that part is the one with a future. The Artifact Was Never the Whole Point There is an old confusion worth naming. We tend to call the finished film "the work," the thing that streams, the thing that is reviewed, the thing that wins or loses a weekend. But anyone who has been inside a production knows the finished film is only the visible part. The work was also the three months an actor spent learning a craft, the village a crew built on location, the town that hosted them, the people who were changed by having been there. The film is the artifact. The making was the event. For most of the industry's history this distinction did not matter much, because you could not have the artifact without the event. To get the film you had to actually make it, somewhere, with people. That is the assumption now coming loose. What AI Changes, and What It Does Not Artificial intelligence is a genuine and remarkable tool. It can translate a film into forty languages, edit and pace and color, generate imagery, and let collaborators across the world build on each other's work. Used well, it expands what filmmakers can do. Social Effects uses it daily, for matching, logistics, and documentation. We are not against it, and this is not a complaint about it. But it is worth being precise about what it does. AI is becoming very good at producing the artifact, the images on the screen. It is not becoming, and is not meant to become, the event. It cannot employ a town. It cannot spend an afternoon with a community. It cannot leave a building behind. A model can generate a convincing image of a place. It cannot give back to one, because it was never in one. The Line Worth Drawing This is not a fear that AI will hollow out film. It is a clearer thought than that. Every powerful tool has a domain where it serves and a domain where it is not the point. As the artifact becomes cheaper and faster to generate, the artifact becomes less of where a film's value lives. What rises in value, by simple contrast, is everything AI cannot touch: a production that physically happened, in a real place, employing real people, leaving real things behind. That is not nostalgia. It is where the durable worth is moving. A film shot in a real town is an economic event for that town, a civic moment, sometimes a piece of lasting infrastructure. A film shot in a real town is an economic event for that town, a civic moment, sometimes a piece of lasting infrastructure. None of that can be simulated, because all of it depends on having actually occurred. Filmmaking as a Civic Act This is the reframe Social Effects is built on. A film is not only a story told on a screen. A production is a temporary institution that arrives in a community, employs its people, uses its spaces, and then leaves. The only question is what it leaves. It can leave a town as it found it, or a little worse, the dumpsters full. Or it can be designed so that the making itself is a gift: surplus rehomed, skills shared, young people brought onto real sets, and at its furthest reach something permanent built that the community keeps. That is Filmanthropy, and it is also, not by accident, the part of filmmaking that AI cannot replicate and cannot replace. A production designed to give back to the place it was made is a production whose value is rooted in the physical world. Why This Is a Future, Not a Defense So the case for Filmanthropy is not only ethical. It is strategic. As the screen-artifact becomes abundant and cheap, the productions that still matter will be the ones that were also events: that happened somewhere, meant something to the place they happened, and left it more whole. Filmmaking earns its future as a civic and creative and infrastructural act, not merely as a supplier of images. The tools will keep getting better. They should. And the work of making a film with other people, in a real place, for the lasting good of that place, will keep being something only people can do. Knowing the difference is not a limitation. It is the whole strategy. Women-owned. WBENC-certified since 2013. What Shannon Schaefer Bart saw on film sets had no department name in 2008. There was no Eco Crew function, no sustainability protocol, no standard procedure for what happened to the materials a production left behind at wrap. Sets went to dumpsters. Food went to trash. Office supplies, furniture, lumber, and costumes went wherever the art department could arrange in the final chaotic days of a shoot, which usually meant nowhere useful. The industry had no mechanism to ask the question, because the question had never been made part of the job. What Bart and Barberg built on A Serious Man in Minneapolis was a proof of concept for something that did not yet have a name. Over ten production weeks, the experiment diverted eleven tons of waste from incineration. Office supplies and furniture went to schools and nonprofits across the Twin Cities. Sets and construction materials went to independent filmmakers rather than into the waste stream. What they built next, in Los Angeles starting in 2009, was a new on-set department: not a consulting add-on, not a green initiative handed down from the studio, but an Eco Crew embedded in the production itself, working from pre-production planning through the final wrap day. The years since have produced a particular kind of operational wisdom. The company survived COVID, when zero-waste targets that had reached ninety-percent landfill diversion dropped to fifty or seventy percent almost overnight as health rules pushed single-use plastics back across the industry. The adaptation, per Barberg's account to Sustainable Brands in July 2024, was to add logistics capabilities, diversify revenue, rent out warehouse space, and stay nimble. There is a vindication in where the founder went next. Bart created a role that did not exist, and the industry's largest engines came looking for it. The function she invented in a Minneapolis production office in 2008, the one with no name and no precedent, is now staffed at the top of the industry by the person who named it. "2024 marks 15 years in business. We've honed our resilient business model based on adaptation and diversification, staying nimble and pivoting quickly. We survived 2020 by adding more logistics capabilities to our wheelhouse and renting out space." Kris Barberg, Executive Director, EcoSet, Sustainable Brands, July 2024 gold verdict-film Why this matters Two women, with no studio behind them, built one of the first real operations for reclaiming what a film production throws away, an embedded crew, a warehouse, a standing department where before there had only been a dumpster. Anyone can found a good idea. The rare thing, the thing that makes EcoSet the proof, is that they kept it running, through a pandemic that gutted the industry overnight, since 2009. Almost no one in this field has earned that word the way they have.

What she saw there, the cases of single-use plastic water bottles, the dumpsters full of struck set at wrap, the food going straight from craft services to the garbage, became the rest of her career. She took her first sustainability role with Big Beach Films that same year, a job that mostly meant sixteen-hour days digging through set trash. The crew, watching her sort recycling from compost over the walkie, started calling her Earth Angel. In 2013 she turned the nickname into a company. Film Biz Recycling's own Brooklyn warehouse would close in less than twelve months, though the work itself would move and carry on elsewhere. The torch was moving between two Brooklyn operators, visibly, in public, in front of the people who had built this field. O'Brien had in fact discovered Film Biz Recycling a few years earlier, while researching a green initiative for Focus Features, the older operation teaching the newer one before either had a name for what they shared. On May 29, 2024, after eleven years and more than a hundred eighty productions, Earth Angel was acquired by TheGreenShot, a Brussels-based company, founded 2021, that folds financial, operational, and environmental tracking for productions into a single platform. The standalone Earth Angel brand was retired. The site that once booked its work now reads, simply, that after an incredible journey to make productions more sustainable, Earth Angel has closed. O'Brien continues inside the merged group as its Chief Impact Manager. The work she built goes on. The name does not, and she chose that trade herself. "I knew what a powerful medium this was and really wanted to help leverage it toward educating folks on these important issues. It wasn't until I got onto my first professional film set where my eyes were really opened to the amount of resource inefficiency that was happening." Emellie O'Brien, Earth Angel founder, Deadline, May 2024 gold verdict-film Why this matters Emellie O'Brien walked onto a film set, saw the waste no one was accounting for, and did the rarest thing in this lineage: she invented the job that did not exist, then built the company around it, and became the East Coast's defining operator in a field she helped name. What makes her story unusual is its ending. Earth Angel did not collapse, and its founder was not quietly hired away. After more than a decade of proving the work, O'Brien folded it into something larger by choice, trading a beloved brand for a longer reach. Lasting a decade is harder than shining for a few years, and choosing your own ending is its own kind of achievement.

He later co-founded the DNA Shoah Project, which uses forensic DNA to reconnect families separated by the Holocaust, and in the early 1980s was among the first to videotape Holocaust survivor testimony. They were signing contracts that obligated the venues to release prepared but unserved food at the end of each show. Goodwill was replaced with obligation. Over the following decades the model extended outward from music to professional sports, more than seventy franchises now, and to the hospitality industry, schools, hospitals, and film and television productions, with NBCUniversal among the named entertainment partners. The organization's film and television work runs under Project: It's a Wrap!, which began in 1997, the first film being The Devil's Own. How much the model has recovered is harder to state cleanly than the organization's headline suggests. Rock and Wrap It Up! says it has fed more than a billion people since 1991, a figure it frames inconsistently across its own materials as people, meals, and pounds. The most recent independently documented numbers are the Environmental Protection Agency's, which in 2009 credited the organization with more than a hundred million pounds of food delivered to more than two hundred million people across five hundred cities, run by roughly six employees on a budget under half a million dollars a year. The Whole Earth Calculator, launched with the NFL at the 2014 Super Bowl, converts pounds of food diverted into meals served and greenhouse gas emissions avoided in a single calculation. Mandelbaum, now in his seventies, is still CEO. He was photographed in 2020 personally unloading food at a Long Island community center during the worst of the COVID year. His reach went past the loading dock and into the law: the language he drafted, working with Representative Jo Ann Emerson and Senator Chuck Schumer, became the basis of the Federal Food Donation Act of 2008, which pushed the federal government to give away its own surplus food rather than trash it. The lineage shows up on film sets directly. Earth Angel, Emellie O'Brien's sustainability company, partnered with Rock and Wrap It Up! on the set of Annie in 2014, redistributing thousands of pounds of catering food through the model Mandelbaum had spent two decades building. In Los Angeles today, EcoSet channels craft services and catering food through Every Day Action, a separate operation reaching the same end by the same logic. The organizations are not linked, but the instinct is one and the same: build the mechanism, and the food finds the people who need it. Film Biz Recycling opened in 2008 in a Fort Greene apartment, moved to a small Long Island City space, and only around 2010 reached the Gowanus warehouse it became known for. The model was simple and unglamorous: a one-stop drop-off for the paint, furniture, wardrobe, set dressing, and raw materials that productions sent to the dump, and a retail floor that worked like the most thoughtfully curated thrift store in the borough, because everything in it had come from a film set. Workshops, green-production seminars, a staff of about a dozen. Roughly sixty percent of everything through the loading dock found its way to local charities, arts programs, and reuse centers, and only two or three percent ever reached a landfill. At peak, ten tons arrived every month. In May 2014, six years in, Film Biz Recycling held the first Golden Dumpster Awards at the warehouse. The Founder's Award for an Individual Displaying Utter Greatness went to Emellie O'Brien of Earth Angel. Radke had opened one of the first operations of its kind on the East Coast, and she was now publicly honoring the person who would carry the category forward. The MPAA, in Radke's account, told her they already had a carting company. They thought she was a garbage operation groveling for a contract. The warehouse was vacated by late June 2015. Still active Eight years on the ground; a documentary in the cut; a foundation now opening to support The correction the record needs Almost everything written about Skater Girl calls it a Netflix film. It was not. The sisters made it independently, financing it themselves and through a private investor, and Netflix acquired the finished film only after seeing it complete. "We made it independently. Netflix came on board when they saw a finished film." The distinction matters more than a footnote, because it changes the meaning of what they did. This was not a streaming giant underwriting a philanthropic gesture out of a marketing budget. Their mother is a nurse. "So the art and the care aspect of it became something that we saw in our home," Vinati says, the two halves of who she and Manjari would become, present in the house before either of them chose a thing. As children they crossed the road to help a woman teaching street kids at the church, not out of virtue but because, as Vinati puts it, "we have free time, this is what we should be doing." As children they crossed the road to help a woman teaching street kids at the church, not out of virtue but because, as Vinati puts it, "we have free time, this is what we should be doing." Skater Girl was their first feature, Manjari directing, Vinati producing, both sisters co-writing with Manjari's husband and co-producer, Emmanuel Pappas. And when they were writing a story about a girl who discovers skateboarding, Manjari said the thing that would define everything after: "We're talking about building a skate park, we should just build a skate park." Emmanuel agreed on the spot. There was no strategy in it, no plan to be change-makers. "We didn't think this would be a blueprint," Vinati says. "We were just like, okay, yeah, we're doing this." The instinct was to keep the giving and the making in the same place. Someone offered them land elsewhere in Rajasthan on the condition that others would manage the park after the shoot, and they said no. "We want the place to be a free community space," Vinati says. "We don't want anyone sabotaging that approach." In retrospect, she knows how it looked: "Anyone would consider that a stupid idea, why are you taking on a responsibility for life?" They took it on anyway. Why Rajasthan, and how they chose They chose the state on purpose. Rajasthan ranked highest on India's Patriarchy Index, a fact the sisters knew before there was a tidy name for it, because, as Vinati says, "we've spent time in India, we recognize the states where women are treated like second-class citizens." It made cinematic sense and it made sense for impact. But choosing a state is not choosing a village, and the sisters spent fifteen days driving across Rajasthan carrying two agendas no ordinary location scout carries: a place to shoot, and land to build on. They traveled with a skateboard, watching how children responded to it. And when they reached the village that felt right, they saw something that settled it: the children there had already made their own skateboards, one little boy dragging a plank on ball bearings across the dirt. That improvised board is in the finished film. "When we saw that," Vinati says, "we just felt: this is where the film needs to be set." The build The build was real construction, and it was hard. The production brought in 100 Ramps, the Bengaluru firm led by pioneering Indian skater Darius Bharucha. Together with a crew of volunteers from across the world, they poured 14,500 square feet of reinforced concrete over 45 days, in the monsoon. It was one of the largest skateparks in India and the first that part of Rajasthan had ever seen. Since then, the skateboarding scene has picked up and now the country boasts of many more skateparks. Even one of the volunteers building it accused the sisters of only caring about their film, and Vinati remembers the sting of it, wanting to tell him he had no idea what their intentions were. She does not blame him, she says: it was so rare for anyone to do this that he had no reference point for it. A skate coach was brought in months ahead of the shoot to train not only the actors but the local children, so that by the time filming began the village kids were skating fearlessly, and most of the young skaters in the film are those children, not imported extras. The production hired more than 350 local people. For the climax, the sisters brought in real skateboarders from across India, because, as Vinati says, "we're making a film about skateboarding and it cannot be done without them." What it asked of her Here is what the research could never show, and what the film's tidy success story leaves out: the years after. The park opened in October 2018. The film wrapped in the spring of 2019 and went up on Netflix in June 2021. But for Vinati, that was not an ending, it was the start of an eight-year commitment that is still going. She set up the Living Grace Foundation so that every donation would move through a clean channel. And then she stayed, and met the full weight of what building something in that village actually meant. She has watched a mother walk into the park with a brick, threatening her own son to make him leave. She has stood in front of a shepherd-community girl who was threatened with being burned alive for the crime of being invited to skate. A farmer once tried to hand her his daughter to raise, "just take my daughter, you'll be able to raise her well" because he could not feed three girls, and she had to find the strength to say no without letting it break her. For years the local men would not meet her eye or speak to her; some addressed her as a man, unused to reporting to a woman. A government official looked her in the face and demanded to know her "selfish agenda" - "why else would you do it?" Two years later, another official told her what she was doing was amazing. It cost money, too, the kind of cost that does not show up in a budget line. "We've personally broken our savings, our mutual funds, stocks," Vinati says, "and continue to put in this." They are only now, cautiously, beginning to open the work to outside support. And it changed her. That some of the Khempur children went on to represent the state is wonderful, but it is not the measure. The measure is whether a child can begin to imagine a different life, the way the girl the sisters met behind a thorn-bush barricade, forbidden to leave her home, had never once been asked what she wanted to do. "No one's ever asked me that question," she told them. That line is in the film. What is still true The park never closed. Skateboards and safety gear are still free. The Living Grace Foundation and the Skate Basti Foundation still keep the lights on. And in April 2021, four of its young skaters, the youngest around ten, most of them leaving their village for the first time in their lives, carried Rajasthan's colors to the national championship in Mohali. The sisters are still filming there, too. They have been documenting the village for eight years and are cutting a documentary from it. And they are already doing it again: their next film will be adopting a similar model in southern India, impact designed in from the first day, the same principle, and once again sport is a theme. Vinati never set out to found a tradition. When told she belonged in a lineage running back a century, from Mary Pickford's relief bucket in 1921 to her own slab in the desert, she recognized it at once. She had simply lived it before anyone gave it a name. "We wanted to make clear that we're not coming here just to make a movie and go away. We were creating something that was going to live beyond the film." docs.title: Sing Sing
docs.text: badge-regen Regenerative A24 · 2024 · Dir. Greg Kwedar Sing Sing The Equity Model Director Greg Kwedar Screenplay Kwedar & Clint Bentley; story also by Clarence Maclin & John Whitfield Lead actor Colman Domingo Pay structure Same SAG scale rate for all cast and crew, star included Equity structure Pro-rata profit participation for entire cast and crew (80+ people) The waterfall 60/40 cast-crew split from first dollar; 50/50 after investors recoup 120% Cast Formerly incarcerated alumni of Rehabilitation Through the Arts (RTA), as themselves Prison release First film released to theaters and prisons at once (A24/RTA/Edovo, Jan 17, 2025) What makes Sing Sing belong in the Regenerative category of the Ledger is not why Greg Kwedar and Clint Bentley made the film. The question is why they structured it the way they did. The film, which premiered at Toronto in 2023 and reached theaters through A24 in 2024, is built around the real Rehabilitation Through the Arts program at Sing Sing Correctional Facility, and its cast is almost entirely formerly incarcerated alumni of that program, playing versions of themselves alongside Colman Domingo in the lead. Years of development produced a film with a specific, unusual deal structure. Everyone on set, from the lead actor to the production assistants, was paid the same SAG scale day rate. And everyone, cast and crew, received a pro-rata share of the producers' equity. Not a charitable gesture, not a nominal points deal, but a real ownership pool: more than eighty people with a stake in the outcome. The mechanics were deliberate. Bentley has described a waterfall in which cast and crew share from the first dollar, and once investors recoup their capital and then some, the split moves to fifty-fifty in perpetuity. Ownership, structured to last beyond the box office. The structure only held because the top of the call sheet agreed to it. Domingo, an Academy Award nominee, took the same rate as a first-day production assistant. Kwedar was blunt about why that mattered: the model does not function unless the number one on the call sheet buys in. He did. And the deeper point was never only about money. Clarence Maclin and John Whitfield, two of the formerly incarcerated men the film is about, share its story credit, and when Sing Sing was nominated for Best Adapted Screenplay, they became the first RTA alumni ever nominated for an Academy Award. The men were not subjects of the story. They were authors of it, and owners of it. Kwedar said as much to Variety at the Brooklyn Academy of Music premiere in June 2024: in a story built around people who had had ownership stripped from them, the whole cast and crew would have literal ownership of their own story. The commitment extended past the deal memo. Sing Sing built permanent equity infrastructure for the people its story was about. Both asked the same question in different registers. Skater Girl: what does this community need that we could also use? Sing Sing: what do these men need, after a lifetime of being taken from, that we could also use? In a film about men whom every system had stripped of agency, the cast did not merely appear in the story. They were paid as equals in it, held equity in it, and in two cases were nominated for an Academy Award for writing it.

docs.title: Motion Picture Relief Fund
docs.text: badge-film Filmanthropic Founded 1921 Motion Picture Relief Fund The Century of Care Founded 1921 Prime mover Mary Pickford (age 29), founding vice-president First president Joseph M. Schenck; Rev. Neal Dodd, administrator 1932 innovation Payroll Pledge Program: 0.5% of wages over $200/week Screen Guild Theatre 1939-1952; star fees funded the campus ($5.2M raised) Campus Woodland Hills (Wasserman Campus), land bought 1940, dedicated 1942 Helped (2020) Nearly 10,000 (MPTF CEO Bob Beitcher, Variety, 2022) Recognition Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award, 2021, the first ever given to an organization Renamed Motion Picture & Television Fund, 1971 The American film industry of 1921 was making a handful of its biggest names extraordinarily wealthy and leaving the rest of its workforce with almost nothing when things went wrong. A worker hurt on set had no compensation. A performer whose career ended had no pension. The industry had the money, the talent, and the audience. It had no mechanism to care for its own. Mary Pickford decided that gap was hers to close. She was twenty-nine, and two years earlier she had co-founded United Artists with Chaplin, Fairbanks, and Griffith, on the conviction that the most powerful people in an industry could remake its economics if they chose to. The Motion Picture Relief Fund was that same conviction turned from the industry's ownership to its welfare. She drove it as its founding vice-president; Joseph Schenck served as its first president and the Reverend Neal Dodd, an Episcopal priest who played clergymen in hundreds of films, ran its day to day. What Pickford built was not a donation. It was a mechanism. The Fund began with coin boxes set out on studio floors, money dropped by the people working that day for the people who weren't. As MPTF still tells it, Pickford kept a little galvanized bucket on her own sets, and if you were lucky enough to be working, she expected you to put something in. By 1932 she had formalized it: the Payroll Pledge Program, under which everyone earning more than two hundred dollars a week gave half of one percent of their wages, automatically. In a single month of 1933, the Fund bought groceries for more than two thousand five hundred film workers and kept seventy-five families from eviction. In 1939 the actor Jean Hersholt, by then the Fund's president, helped launch the Screen Guild Theatre, a weekly radio program on which the biggest names in Hollywood performed and donated their fees. It ran until 1952 and raised more than five million dollars, and that money bought land. In Woodland Hills, on what had been forty-odd acres of walnut and orange groves, the Fund broke ground in 1941 and dedicated the Motion Picture Country House in 1942: a place for the industry's elders and most vulnerable to grow old among their own. docs.text: what had been forty-odd acres of walnut and orange groves, the Fund broke ground in 1941 and dedicated the Motion Picture Country House in 1942: a place for the industry's elders and most vulnerable to grow old among their own. It operates still, today the Wasserman Campus, under the name the Fund took in 1971, the Motion Picture & Television Fund. Per Variety's centennial reporting, nearly ten thousand people received its help in 2020 alone. There is a circle worth closing here. The Academy's award for humanitarian work is named for Jean Hersholt, the man who ran this Fund for eighteen years and raised the money that built its campus. In 2021, for the first time in its history, the Academy gave that award not to a person but to an organization: to the Motion Picture Relief Fund itself. The honor named for the man came home to the institution he had built. A hundred years after a twenty-nine-year-old passed a bucket on a silent-film set, the industry's own highest body of recognition bent its rules to say that the care had been worth as much as the art. "Actors are only ever between engagements." Mary Pickford's reported insistence that the Woodland Hills home be called a House, not a Home (MPTF history) gold verdict-film Our Take In 1921 the question was not what the industry should do for itself. It was what one of its most powerful people could build with the leverage she had while she had it. Mary Pickford answered with infrastructure that has now lasted a century: a working campus that still takes people in, a payroll pledge that made giving a normal line on the check, and, in 2021, an Academy Award given for the first time not to a person but to the institution she founded. The Motion Picture Relief Fund is proof that philanthropy designed in early enough, and backed by enough power to stick, can outlast everyone who built it.

docs.title: The Lord of the Rings
docs.text: badge-sust Sustainable / Adjacent New Line Cinema · 2001–2003 / The Hobbit · Warner Bros. · 2012–2014 The Lord of the Rings The Set That Became a Country Site Alexander family farm, Matamata, Waikato, NZ (approx. 1,250 acres) Set area Approx. 12 acres Site discovered Aerial location search, 1998 Original Hobbiton 37-39 temporary hobbit holes (1999); mostly cleared after filming Facades left ~17 bare plywood facades survived (rain halted demolition) Tours began 2002 (Russell Alexander, son of original owner Ian) Permanent rebuild 2010-2011 for The Hobbit; 44 permanent hobbit holes today Ownership today Alexander family and Peter Jackson, roughly 50/50 Visitors in 2019 650,000 (pre-Covid peak) Tourism value ~$630M NZD/yr film-influenced visitor spend (Tourism NZ, 2019) When the Lord of the Rings crew finished filming the Shire and moved on, they left behind, on the Alexander family's working sheep and beef farm in Matamata, the bones of Hobbiton. The set had been built of plywood and polystyrene, meant to be temporary. An attempt to clear it was halted by heavy rain, and roughly seventeen bare hobbit-hole facades were left standing in the paddock, with the understanding that the crew would return to finish the job. The film was done. The lease was satisfied. The Alexanders were left with seventeen movie-set remnants and a decision. They kept them. Russell Alexander, a son of the farmer the location scouts had first approached in 1998, opened tours in 2002 and spent years turning curious foot traffic into a working tourism business, through the family's own initiative. The production that had found the farm by air, sent the New Zealand Army to build a 1.5-kilometer access road, and raised the most beloved set in modern cinema on a sheep paddock had left with no obligation to the family's economic future. The family engineered that future themselves. Then the value the family had proven drew the production back. When Peter Jackson returned in 2009 to prepare The Hobbit, Hobbiton was rebuilt, this time in stone and timber, meant to last. Construction across 2010 and 2011 produced the forty-four permanent hobbit holes and the Green Dragon Inn that visitors see today. And the deal had changed: Jackson became a fifty-percent partner in the tourism operation. The set that a production had once walked away from was now one the filmmaker co-owned. By 2019, Hobbiton drew 650,000 visitors, and Tourism New Zealand estimated that film-influenced travel was worth around 630 million New Zealand dollars a year to the country. There is a shadow on the case, and it has been named on the record. Scholars including Misha Kavka, Stephen Turner, and Alice Te Punga Somerville have argued that the Tolkien-tourism wave rebranded the New Zealand landscape as Middle-earth and, in doing so, overwrote the land's own history, including its precolonial Maori history, in the story sold to visitors. It now employs hundreds and draws visitors from every continent. Hobbiton is the largest residual community asset in modern film history, and it became one almost by accident, so completely that once the family had proven the value, the production came back to buy in, with Peter Jackson taking a fifty-percent stake in the business itself.
